"Lump" as a verb has two distinct and important meanings. They are quite different from each other, so let's look at them one by one.
Meaning 1: To put different things or people into one group

This is the most common and important meaning. When you lump things together, you treat several different things as if they are all the same — you group them together, often in a way that ignores the real differences between them.

Think of it like this: imagine you have apples, oranges, mangoes, and bananas. Instead of talking about each fruit separately, you just wave your hand and say, "These are all just fruit — same thing." You have lumped them all together.

Examples:

  • "Don't lump all teenagers together — they're all very different people."
  • "The teacher lumped the weak students and the strong students into one class."
  • "He lumped all his expenses together and called it one bill."

The important nuance here

Lumping things together is usually negative or unfair. It carries the idea that the person doing the grouping is being lazy, careless, or oversimplistic. They are ignoring real and important differences.

For example:

  • "Stop lumping me in with those people — I'm nothing like them!"

Here, the speaker is upset because someone has grouped them with others unfairly, as if they are all the same.

Common patterns you'll see:

  • lump together → "They lumped the two issues together, but they're completely unrelated."
  • lump something with something → "Don't lump my idea in with his — mine is totally different."
  • lump someone in with someone → "She got lumped in with the beginners even though she had experience."
Meaning 2: To put up with something unpleasant (whether you like it or not)

This meaning is mostly used in informal British English, and almost always appears in one specific, very famous phrase:

"Like it or lump it."

This phrase means: whether you like it or not, you have no choice but to accept it. There is nothing you can do about the situation, so you just have to tolerate it — even if it bothers you.

Examples:

  • "The new rules are in place. You can like it or lump it."
  • "I know you're not happy with the decision, but you'll just have to lump it."

The feel of this phrase

It is a bit blunt and unsympathetic. When someone says "lump it" to you, they are basically saying: "Stop complaining. Accept it. Move on." There's a slight dismissiveness to it — the person saying it doesn't really care whether you're unhappy. The situation is the situation.

It's worth noting that in this meaning, you almost never say "lump it" without the "like it or" in front of it, or without some context making the "accept it" meaning clear. You wouldn't typically say "I lumped the bad weather" — that would sound strange. The phrase is mostly fixed as "like it or lump it" or just "lump it" in response to a complaint.
How to keep both meanings straight

Here's a simple way to remember both:

Simple reminder
Meaning 1You lump different things into one pile — you group them together, usually ignoring their differences.
Meaning 2You lump a bad situation — you swallow it, you accept it, you live with it.
A few more natural examples to cement it all

Meaning 1 (grouping):

  • "It's wrong to lump all immigrants together as if they're one group with the same story."
  • "The report lumped several completely different crimes into a single category, which made the data misleading."
  • "She hates being lumped together with her siblings — she feels like people never see her as an individual."

Meaning 2 (accept it):

  • "The flight is delayed by three hours. Like it or lump it — there's nothing anyone can do."
  • "He wasn't happy with his assigned seat, but he just had to lump it."

To lump means either:

  1. To group different things together as if they're all the same (usually unfairly or carelessly), or
  2. To accept something unpleasant that you have no power to change — "like it or lump it."

The first meaning is far more widely used and appears in all kinds of contexts worldwide. The second is informal, mostly British, and almost always appears as part of the fixed phrase "like it or lump it."
